reconcile.connective: Defenders read the destruction oracles not as abrogating the brother-command but as judging Edom for its own treachery, the very enmity Deuteronomy told both peoples to drop.

discrepancy.connective: Bert Dicou documents the unresolved literary tension head-on: the same Edom that Genesis and Deuteronomy frame as Israel's kindred "brother" is, in Obadiah and the prophetic oracles, the archetypal antagonist marked for total destruction, a duality the texts hold together without reconciling.

skeptic.name: Bert Dicou
skeptic.work: Edom, Israel's Brother and Antagonist: The Role of Edom in Biblical Prophecy and Story
skeptic.attribution: Bert Dicou, Edom, Israel's Brother and Antagonist: The Role of Edom in Biblical Prophecy and Story (JSOTSup 169; Sheffield: JSOT Press, 1994)

excerpts.excerpt_text: But the Jews had a divine warrant to reign over the Edomites, for that therefore they ought not to have made reprisals; and it was the more disingenuous for them to retain the old enmity when God had particularly commanded his people to forget it. Deu 23:7, Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Matthew Henry quotes Deut 23:7 directly against the Edom-destruction oracle and harmonizes: Edom is judged not in defiance of the brother-command but for clinging to the very enmity God told both peoples to forget; the destruction is read as desert for Edom's own treachery, not arbitrary genocide.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Ezekiel 25:12-14
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats this exact tension on the row, citing Deut 23:7 ('Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite') alongside the Edom oracle and harmonizing the destruction as just recompense for Edom's own revenge against its brother Judah.
